# Why

Spike-in controls are added at amounts we know. spikeWatch uses those
known amounts to score every run, the same way every time, and to watch
those scores across runs to show drift. The charts are exploratory, not validated run-release alarms:
at the default limits with a 20-run baseline, a CUSUM or EWMA chart of `slope`, `residSD` or `offset` raised a
false alarm within 20 monitored runs in 15.7% to 19.2% of simulated drift-free series in the
base family, and in 36.7% to 83.4% when runs were correlated (up to 35.2% and 87.3% for the
displayed U-T and U-F union charts), so check their limits on your own runs first.
In the package's simulation study, charts of the known-amount figures did not beat
the best truth-free charts, such as `profileResidSD`, under the precommitted rule,
apart from one EWMA gain, which had a higher false-alarm rate than its truth-free
comparator in all 12 of its family and horizon cells and is not yet tested on fresh
seeds (see the README). These figures come from the validation in the package's source
repository (the `validation/` folder at the URL in DESCRIPTION, with its plan, scripts
and outputs; the main study ran at commit d7dfeb0 and addendum 2's outputs were committed at
5fb0966), which is not part of the package tarball.

The known amounts live in an assay beside the measurements. That one idea
covers both kinds of design:

* feature-level designs, where each spike has its own amount, such as the
  ERCC RNA mixes;
* sample-level designs, where the amount changes from sample to sample,
  such as a UPS1 or peptide dilution series.

# Installation

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE))
    install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install("spikeWatch")
```

# A series of runs

`simulateSpikeRuns()` makes count data for runs of one ERCC mix, with
sequencing depth that changes from run to run. Here the dose response
compresses from run 31 on: high spikes read a little lower and low spikes
a little higher.

```{r simulate}
library(spikeWatch)
ercc <- erccDesign()
set.seed(7)
runs <- simulateSpikeRuns(ercc, nRuns = 40, mix = "Mix1", driftAt = 31,
                          driftType = "slope", driftSize = -0.1)
runs
```

The experiment already has its truth attached. For your own data, build or
load a design and call `addTruth()`; see the next section.

# Per-run accuracy

```{r metrics}
m <- runMetrics(runs, baseline = 20)
head(m, 3)
attr(m, "minAmount")
```

`slope` near 1 means the measured values follow the known amounts.
`minAmount` keeps spikes near the detection limit out of the fit: they are
seen only when their count happens to be high, which would pull the slope
down and tie it to depth. By default it is the smallest amount at and
above which every spike was seen in every baseline run, so the fit range
is chosen from good runs only and stays the same for every run. The
detection limit `lod` always uses every spike, and is `NA` with a reason
in `lodStatus` when the data cannot support it.

```{r doseplot, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
plotDoseResponse(runs, 1, minAmount = attr(m, "minAmount"))
```

# Drift across runs

The first 20 runs are the baseline. A CUSUM chart on the slope flags the
drift:

```{r chart, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 3.5}
ch <- driftChart(m, "slope", baseline = 20, method = "cusum")
firstSignal(ch)
plotDrift(ch, "Dose-response slope, CUSUM")
```

`driftChart()` also offers EWMA and Shewhart charts, and can chart any
column of `runMetrics()`: `residSD` for precision, `offset` for overall
response, `lod` for sensitivity at the low end.

The default limits (`h = 5` for CUSUM, `L = 3` for EWMA) treat the
baseline's centre and spread as exact. With 20 baseline runs they are
not, and the chart gives more false alarms than those limits suggest.
The package's validation reports how many, so read a first signal from
a short baseline with that in mind.

`profileMetrics()` gives the figures a lab could chart without the known
amounts, from the profile of the same spikes over the baseline runs. They
are the comparison the package's validation uses for the truth-based
figures, and it reports both.

```{r profile}
p <- profileMetrics(runs, baseline = 20)
round(tail(p$profileSlope), 3)
```

# Your own data

Rows of the experiment must be named by spike identifier, and `colData`
must say which mix each sample received:

```{r own}
library(SummarizedExperiment)
counts <- assay(runs, "counts")
se <- SummarizedExperiment(list(counts = counts),
                           colData = DataFrame(mix = rep("Mix1", 40)))
se <- addTruth(se, ercc, mix = "mix")
identical(assay(se, "expected"), assay(runs, "expected"))
```

For a dilution series, give each sample a dose and the design one amount
per spike:

```{r dose}
d <- spikeDesign(c("p1", "p2", "p3"), amount = c(1, 1, 1), unit = "fmol")
x <- matrix(c(10, 12, 9, 100, 118, 95), nrow = 3,
            dimnames = list(c("p1", "p2", "p3"), c("low", "high")))
s <- SummarizedExperiment(list(area = x),
                          colData = DataFrame(fmol = c(0.5, 5)))
s <- addTruth(s, d, dose = "fmol")
runMetrics(s)[, c("run", "nDetected", "offset")]
```

# Fold-change accuracy

With samples from two mixes, `ratioAccuracy()` compares measured and
expected log2 ratios, spike by spike and per expected ratio:

```{r ratio}
set.seed(1)
a <- simulateSpikeRuns(ercc, nRuns = 3, mix = "Mix1")
set.seed(2)
b <- simulateSpikeRuns(ercc, nRuns = 3, mix = "Mix2")
colnames(b) <- paste0("b", 1:3)
ratioAccuracy(cbind(a, b), 1:3, 4:6)$summary
```

# Related packages

Other Bioconductor packages work with spike-ins or run-to-run quality
control. erccdashboard scores one experiment against the ERCC ratio
mixtures (AUC, LODR and ratio bias between two samples). MSstatsQC charts
per-peptide run metrics such as retention time and peak area over time,
with X, moving range and CUSUM charts and change point estimation, from a
guide set of good runs. Anaquin analyses sequins. spikeWatch scores each
run against the known spike amounts and charts those scores; it does not
replace a full QC platform.
